output:
# PRD: In-app substitution approvals ## 1. Problem When an item is out of stock (11.8% of orders, averaging 1.7 items each), the shopper picks a substitute alone and the customer finds out at the door. **23% of substitutes are rejected at the door**, which means a wasted item, a refund, and an unhappy customer. Shoppers also have no way to ask. ## 2. Goals and success metrics | Metric | Baseline | Target (proposed) | |---|---|---| | Substitutes rejected after delivery | 23% | ≤10% | | Requests answered within the window | 74% (pilot, 5 min) | ≥75% | | Median shopper pick-to-checkout time | 34 min | ≤36 min | | Restricted items substituted | n/a | 0 | | Customers charged more than the original price | n/a | 0 | For sizing, 11.8% × 1.7 ≈ 0.2 requests per order. ## 3. Non-goals - Changing the Customer Terms or pricing policy (see the Finance decision below). - Substituting restricted items. - Auto-ranking substitutes with ML. V1 uses shopper judgement plus a catalogue filter. - Live chat between shopper and customer. ## 4. Decisions on the window and default **Window: 5 minutes per item, running in parallel with picking.** - Pilot responses were 38% within 1 min, 61% within 3 min and 74% within 5 min. The other 26% never responded before checkout, so **no one responded after minute 5**. A longer window gains nothing. - A 3-minute window would forfeit 13 points of responders. - The shopper keeps picking while the clock runs, so the window costs little against a 34-minute pick. - A reminder push goes out at 3:00. **Default on no response: remove the item and refund it. Do not auto-approve.** - 26% of requests got no answer, and silence is not consent. - Shopper-chosen substitutes are already rejected 23% of the time, so auto-approval would knowingly deliver an unwanted item to roughly 1 in 4 of those customers. - Refund is always safe and always within the Terms. - The cost is lost sales, so we will test an opt-in "accept like-for-like substitutes at or below the original price" preference (see open questions). ## 5. Stakeholder requests | Request | Decision | |---|---| | **Ops (John Stiles):** 60-second timeout with auto-approve, because the median customer responds in under a minute. | **Declined.** The premise is wrong. Only 38% respond within 1 minute, and the median is about 2 minutes (interpolated). A 60s window would leave 62% of requests unanswered, and auto-approving them recreates the 23% door-rejection problem. His real concern, shoppers waiting, is solved by async design (FR-4). | | **Finance (Richard Miles):** charge the substitute's shelf price when it costs more. | **Escalated to Legal and Finance; not in v1.** Published Terms §7.3 say customers "will never pay more than the price of the item you ordered." Charging more would breach our own terms. V1 charges the lower of the two prices. Any change needs a Terms revision with notice and explicit per-item consent. To reduce margin loss now, the shopper UI prioritises substitutes priced at or below the original. | ## 6. User stories **Customer** - As a customer, I want to approve or reject a substitute before it is bought, so I'm not surprised at the door. - As a customer, I want to see exactly what I'll pay, so I'm never charged more than I ordered. - As a customer, I want to know what happens if I don't answer, so I can decide whether to act. - As a customer, I want to choose a different substitute if I dislike the proposed one. **Shopper** - As a shopper, I want to propose a substitute in seconds and keep picking, so I'm not idle. - As a shopper, I want to see each request's status (pending, approved, rejected, expired), so I know what to buy. - As a shopper, I want a hard time limit, so a silent customer never blocks my checkout. ## 7. Functional requirements 1. **FR-1 Propose.** The shopper marks an item out of stock and selects a substitute from the catalogue. The customer gets a push notification and in-app screen. 2. **FR-2 Restricted items.** Age-restricted (alcohol, tobacco) and pharmacy items cannot be proposed. The shopper UI offers only "refund item", and the customer is notified. 3. **FR-3 Customer screen.** It shows the original item, the substitute, the price the customer pays, a countdown, and the default outcome. Actions are Approve, Reject, and Choose another. 4. **FR-4 Async picking.** Each request has its own 5:00 timer. The shopper continues picking. Checkout is blocked only until every request is resolved or expired, so the maximum wait is 5 minutes. 5. **FR-5 Reminder.** One reminder push at 3:00 remaining, if still unanswered. 6. **FR-6 Pricing.** Charge = min(substitute price, original price). The screen shows the shelf price and the amount charged. If the substitute is cheaper, the customer pays the lower price. For weighted or multi-pack items, cap the line total at the original line total. 7. **FR-7 Reject.** The item is removed and refunded. The shopper may propose one further substitute per item, so at most two proposals, each with its own 5-minute window. 8. **FR-8 Choose another.** Show up to 3 in-stock alternatives priced at or below the original. A selection counts as approval and is sent to the shopper. It does not reset the timer. 9. **FR-9 Expiry.** At 0:00 the item is removed and refunded. The shopper and customer are notified. 10. **FR-10 Logging.** Log every request, response time, outcome and price charged, for metrics and audit. ## 8. Edge cases - **Multiple out-of-stock items:** one notification groups them, with independent per-item decisions and timers. - **Late response:** show "This request expired. The item was refunded." Offer no reorder inside the order. - **App closed or notifications off:** fall back to SMS for the reminder. Otherwise the default applies. - **Substitute goes out of stock after approval:** treat it as a new request. - **Shopper reaches the final item with others unresolved:** wait up to the window, then check out. - **Whole order consists of restricted items:** refund only, with no approval flow. - **Customer approves at exactly 0:00:** the server timestamp decides. - **Promotional or multi-buy original price:** the cap uses the price actually in the customer's basket. ## 9. Open questions 1. Legal and Finance: is there appetite to revise §7.3, and what consent model would apply? 2. Should we A/B-test the opt-in "like-for-like at or below price" standing preference against the refund default? 3. How representative is the pilot (one store, 1,200 requests)? Does response vary by time of day or customer segment? 4. Are the ≤10% door-rejection and ≤36 min targets right? Confirm with Ops. 5. Is SMS fallback cost justified by response uplift? 6. How are shoppers compensated for any residual wait? --- ## Prototype ```html Substitute approval

Approve a substitute?

Maya, your shopper, is still picking your order.

4:32 left to respond
You ordered
🥛
Oat Barista Drink 1L
$3.49 · Out of stock
Maya suggests
🥛
Store-brand Oat Drink 1L
Shelf price $3.79
You pay $3.49

You never pay more than the price of the item you ordered. We cover the $0.30 difference.

Choose another
  • Soy Barista Drink 1L$3.29
  • Almond Drink 1L$3.49
  • Oat Drink 1L (organic)$3.49

If you don't respond: when the timer reaches 0:00 we'll skip this item and refund it. You won't be charged for it, and no substitute will be bought.

``` ## Design rationale The countdown sits at the top, in a warm colour, so urgency is clear before any decision. Original and substitute are stacked and labelled. The old item is struck through and marked out of stock, and the substitute has a green border, so the comparison takes seconds. The price line says "You pay $3.49" in the largest type, with the shelf price in small text, so the cap in Terms §7.3 is visible and no one infers a higher charge. Approve is the dominant button. Reject names its consequence ("remove & refund"). "Choose another" expands in place, so customers don't lose context. The no-response outcome is spelled out in plain language, because the default is refund, not auto-approval. Buttons are at least 50px tall with visible focus states. The timer works without JavaScript, because the static value is already in the markup.
